Lessons.Title: The Size of Angles in Degrees
ExplanationParagraphs: The original IM/KH 2021 Grade 4 Unit 7 Lesson 8 introduces degrees as units of angle measurement through a ray's turning. One FULL revolution around a fixed endpoint is 360°. A half turn is 180°, a quarter turn is 90°, and three quarter turns is 270°.

Warm-up (10 minutes) — What Do You Know about 360? Students name familiar uses and make sense of full-turn degrees. Teacher checks discussion instead of treating an arithmetic completion as source participation.

Activity 1 (15 minutes) — A Full Turn. Start one ray at a chosen direction and rotate it once around its vertex until it returns to the starting direction; the accumulated TURN is 360°, even though the two final rays coincide. A 120° turn is one third of a full turn and a 180° turn is one half.

Activity 2 (20 minutes) — Make a Measuring Tool. The source provides a semicircular sheet with reference 120° and 180° from a baseline ray. Construct and use a teacher-supervised paper tool; position its centre on the angle vertex and align a baseline with one arm. Do not pretend the original publisher semicircle or its diagram has been embedded here.

Students compare angle size to benchmarks, rather than using hand-drawn ray length. Estimates should be justified using 90°, 120°, 180° and fractions of 360°; exact measurement or photocopied publisher diagram fidelity are not established by a digital number alone.

Independent first-party Cool-down (5 minutes, NOT publisher original Estimate Angle Size in Degrees): what fraction of a whole 360° rotation is 270°? Explain 270/360 = 3/4. Teacher checks any sketch and explanation.

First-party digital Practice includes selected degree turns 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 270°, and 360°. It asks for either numerator or denominator of the fraction of a full turn in lowest terms, or the remaining degrees to finish a full revolution. It does not grade student-constructed semicircle tools or angle estimates from unpublished source graphics.

KeyConcepts.Title: Degrees around a whole rotation
KeyConcepts.Definition: One complete turn of a ray around a fixed vertex equals 360 degrees.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Quarter turn = 360°/4 = 90°; half turn = 180°; three-quarter turn = 270°.
KeyConcepts.Example: A ray turns 270°: that is 3/4 of a full revolution, with 90° still to turn.

KeyConcepts.Title: Angles as fractions of one turn
KeyConcepts.Definition: Any rotation θ degrees is θ/360 of a full turn; write the fraction in simplest terms.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Reduce numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Benchmark estimation and measuring tool
KeyConcepts.Definition: A paper semicircle carries known reference turns such as 120° and 180° from a baseline.
KeyConcepts.Rule: To compare an original drawn angle, locate the common vertex and orient the baseline of a real, aligned tool; teacher checks the actual drawing.
KeyConcepts.Example: Estimate whether a shown opening is smaller or larger than the known 120° benchmark; no hidden diagram is numerically inferred.

WorkedExamples.Title: A complete revolution
WorkedExamples.Question: A ray rotates all the way back to its starting direction. How many degrees has it turned?
WorkedExamples.Method: One turn has 360 equal one-degree subdivisions.
Steps: Rotate the ray through one complete circle.
It returns to its starting direction after 360° of cumulative turning.
WorkedExamples.Check: A full-turn rotation is not the zero-turn path, even when the end direction matches.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fraction of turn for 120°
WorkedExamples.Question: What fraction of a full 360° revolution is a 120° turn?

WorkedExamples.Title: Fraction of turn for 270°
WorkedExamples.Question: How much of a 360° turn is 270°? How many degrees remain?
WorkedExamples.Method: Reduce the turn fraction and subtract from 360.
Steps: Three quarter turns plus one quarter turn make one full turn.

WorkedExamples.Title: Half-circle source measuring tool (teacher-scored)
WorkedExamples.Question: The 2021 source provides a half-circle paper measuring tool showing 120° and 180° from a baseline. Explain and check their relation.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use an authorised original or independently drawn teacher tool.
Steps: Align the baseline ray with the teacher's paper semicircle.
Inspect actual source reference markings: 120° corresponds to one third of 360°; 180° to one half.
Explain their sizes and draw or trace the represented turns; teacher checks tool scale and printed image.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 120° = 1/3 full turn; 180° = 1/2 full turn, subject to actual diagram review.
WorkedExamples.Check: No digital angle estimate or copied source semicircle is claimed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent first-party Cool-down (teacher-reviewed explanation)
WorkedExamples.Question: What fraction of a full turn is 270°?
Steps: Explain 3/4 is three quarters of the full circle.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is not the inaccessible publisher Cool-down.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a ray that returns to its starting direction as zero TURN.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Direction and cumulative turn are different: a ray can rotate a full 360° and end in its initial position.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count the motion through the complete circle, not just the matching endpoints.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a 120° paper angle is the same as a 180° semicircle.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 120° is one third of a 360° turn, while 180° is one half.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use benchmark fractions and inspect source tool markings when available.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Automatically claiming numerical Practice validates paper-tool construction and original visual estimation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The publisher activity requires the learner to physically align, make and compare a real measuring tool.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher assesses alignment, scale, drawings and reasoning separately.

SummaryPoints: A full turn is 360°; quarter=90°, half=180°, three-quarter=270°.
120° is a third of a turn, 180° is half, 270° is three quarters.
Source paper measuring-tool construction with 120°/180° labels and original angle estimates are teacher-led.
First-party exact Practice assesses fractional benchmarks and remaining degrees only; no source image/Cool-down parity is asserted.
